nodes.label: The Middle Assyrian Kingdom
nodes.full: The kingdom this empire is built from — the annalistic ideology, the holy-war theology, the deportation system, the god Ashur, and the King List, all carried through the dark age. See assyria-1400bc-1050bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio assyria-1400bc-1050bc.

nodes.label: The Neo-Babylonian Empire
nodes.full: Nabopolassar's Babylon, which breaks free in 626, allies with the Medes to destroy Assyria, and inherits its western empire. See babylon-1155bc-539bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-1155bc-539bc.

nodes.label: The Medes
nodes.full: The Iranian people Assyria raided for horses for two centuries, coalescing under Cyaxares into a kingdom that joins Babylon in the campaign that ends Assyria.
nodes.src: background — the 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle'; Herodotus I.102–106.

nodes.label: The Kingdom of Judah
nodes.full: The small Levantine kingdom left alone after Assyria destroyed its northern neighbour, its siege by Sennacherib and the reckoning that followed being the crucible of biblical monotheism.
nodes.src: background — 2 Kings 18–25; see the folio egypt-1200bc-664bc for the wider Levant.

nodes.label: Urartu
nodes.full: The fortress kingdom around Lake Van — Assyria's most serious rival for a century and a half, and the contested gateway to the horse and metal trade of the highlands.
nodes.src: background — Paul Zimansky, 'Ecology and Empire: The Structure of the Urartian State' (1985).

nodes.label: The recovery — Ashur-dan II to Adad-nirari II
nodes.full: Beginning with Ashur-dan II, a run of kings clawed the kingdom back from the dark age — retaking the Jazira from the Aramaean statelets, resettling the abandoned land, rebuilding the towns, and restoring the yearly campaign as the rhythm of the state. Their inscriptions frame it as a return: bringing 'the exhausted people of Assyria' home and pushing the border back out to where the fathers had held it.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC I' (RIMA 2, 1991); Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction' (2015).

nodes.label: Ashurnasirpal II — the terror and the showpiece
nodes.full: Ashurnasirpal II drove west to the Mediterranean with a cruelty his own annals dwell on — flayed rebels, pillars of severed heads, cities burned. He then moved the capital to Kalhu and built the Northwest Palace, its state rooms lined with carved stone reliefs, and marked its opening with a ten-day banquet for 69,574 people, itemised on a stone stele. Calculated terror abroad and calculated magnificence at home became the Assyrian method.
nodes.src: Grayson, RIMA 2 (1991); the Banquet Stele and the Northwest Palace from the Nimrud excavations (Layard; Mallowan).

nodes.label: Shalmaneser III — the long reach and the first check
nodes.full: Shalmaneser III campaigned for thirty-four years. At Qarqar in 853 he met a coalition of a dozen Levantine kings — Damascus, Hamath, Ahab of Israel — and, though his annals claim victory, he did not break through the west for years. His Black Obelisk shows Jehu of Israel prostrate with tribute. He brought Babylon under Assyrian protection. His last years brought a great revolt and the start of the 'age of the magnates'.
nodes.src: Grayson, RIMA 3 (1996); the Kurkh Monolith and the Black Obelisk (British Museum).

nodes.label: The age of the magnates
nodes.full: For eighty years the kings were weak and the empire was run by its great provincial governors — men like the commander-in-chief Shamshi-ilu, who campaigned and set up monuments in his own name. Plague, a total solar eclipse taken as an omen of catastrophe, and repeated revolt marked the period. Assyria shrank back toward its heartland, and the crown's authority nearly dissolved.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman on the period; the Saba'a and Tell al-Rimah stelae; the Assyrian eponym chronicle for 763 (the Bur-Sagale eclipse).

nodes.label: Tiglath-Pileser III — the refounder
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser III took the throne in a coup and rebuilt the state from the ground up: he broke the over-mighty provinces into small districts under directly appointed governors, many of them eunuchs; he made the army a permanent professional force; he systematised two-way mass deportation; he annexed conquered kingdoms as provinces instead of leaving native vassals; and he took the throne of Babylon himself. He is the true founder of the imperial system.
nodes.src: Hayim Tadmor & Shigeo Yamada, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III' (RINAP 1, 2011); Radner (2015).

nodes.label: Sargon II — the usurper who named himself for Akkad
nodes.full: Sargon II seized the throne in the disorder after Shalmaneser V and adopted a throne-name recalling Sargon of Akkad. He destroyed the Kingdom of Israel and deported its people, crushed the rival kingdom of Urartu, fought Merodach-Baladan for Babylon, and built an entirely new capital from bare ground, Dur-Sharrukin. Then he was killed in battle in Anatolia and his body was never recovered — a disaster his son read as divine punishment.
nodes.src: Grant Frame, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Sargon II' (RINAP 2, 2021); the 'Letter to the God Ashur' on the eighth campaign against Urartu.

nodes.label: Sennacherib — Nineveh and the razing of Babylon
nodes.full: Sennacherib abandoned his father's ill-omened new city and made Nineveh the greatest capital in the world — the 'Palace Without Rival', an 80-kilometre canal system, and a terraced garden that some identify with the 'Hanging Gardens'. He besieged Hezekiah's Jerusalem in 701 and pulled back without taking it. And in 689 he did the unthinkable: he razed Babylon, flooded the site, and carried its gods away. His own sons murdered him.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson & Jamie Novotny, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Sennacherib' (RINAP 3, 2012–14); John Malcolm Russell, 'Sennacherib's Palace Without Rival at Nineveh' (1991).

nodes.label: Esarhaddon — the rebuilder and the conqueror of Egypt
nodes.full: Esarhaddon won a civil war against his brothers, then reversed his father's great crime by rebuilding Babylon — a theological about-face carefully justified in his inscriptions. In 671 he invaded Egypt, took Memphis, and drove out the Kushite pharaoh Taharqa, briefly making Assyria a two-continent empire. Sick, anxious and hemmed in by omens, he bound the whole empire by oath to accept his sons as heirs — the Succession Treaty.
nodes.src: Erle Leichty, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Esarhaddon' (RINAP 4, 2011); Simo Parpola & Kazuko Watanabe, 'Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths' (SAA 2, 1988).

nodes.label: Ashurbanipal — the scholar-king at the peak
nodes.full: Under Ashurbanipal the empire reached its greatest extent. He sacked Thebes in 663; he crushed and finally destroyed Elam, sacking Susa in 646; he fought a four-year war against his own brother, the king of Babylon, that ended with the brother dead in the burning palace. He also built at Nineveh the first systematic library, a project to gather every kind of written knowledge — and he boasted, uniquely for a king, that he could read it.
nodes.src: Jamie Novotny & Joshua Jeffers, 'The Royal Inscriptions of Ashurbanipal' (RINAP 5, 2018–); the library in Frame & George, 'The Royal Libraries of Nineveh' (2005).

nodes.label: The twenty-year collapse
nodes.full: After Ashurbanipal's death the empire fell apart with astonishing speed. His sons Ashur-etil-ilani and Sin-shar-ishkun fought over the throne; Babylon broke free under Nabopolassar in 626; the Medes under Cyaxares allied with him. Ashur fell in 614, Nineveh was sacked in 612, and a last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, made a doomed stand at Harran with Egyptian help. By 609 the largest empire the world had known simply no longer existed.
nodes.src: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' (ABC 3); the prophet Nahum; the speed of the collapse discussed in Eckart Frahm (ed.), 'A Companion to Assyria' (2017).

nodes.label: The queens — Sammu-ramat and Naqia
nodes.full: Assyrian royal women could hold real power. Sammu-ramat, mother of Adad-nirari III, appears on a boundary stele beside her son and campaigned with the army — she is the historical seed of the Greek legend of Semiramis. A century later Naqia, wife of Sennacherib and mother of Esarhaddon, engineered her son's and then her grandson's succession and imposed a loyalty oath on the empire in her own name.
nodes.src: The Pazarcık stele (Sammu-ramat); Sarah Melville, 'The Role of Naqia/Zakutu in Sargonid Politics' (1999); the 'Zakutu Treaty' (SAA 2, no. 8).

nodes.label: The reconquest of the west and Qarqar
nodes.full: Ashurnasirpal II reached the Mediterranean and washed his weapons in the sea; Shalmaneser III tried to break through the Levantine kingdoms and, at Qarqar on the Orontes in 853, fought the largest coalition Assyria had yet faced — Damascus, Hamath, Israel and nine others, fielding thousands of chariots. Assyria claimed the field but could not hold the west for another decade, when Damascus finally submitted and Jehu of Israel paid tribute.
nodes.src: Grayson, RIMA 2–3; the Kurkh Monolith account of Qarqar; the Black Obelisk.

nodes.label: The long war with Urartu
nodes.full: Urartu, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van, was Assyria's most serious rival for a century and a half — a fortress state that contested the northern frontier and the horse and metal trade of the highlands. Sargon II's eighth campaign in 714, described at length in a 'letter to the god Ashur', shattered Urartu's army and sacked the temple-city of Musasir. Urartu survived but never threatened Assyria again.
nodes.src: The 'Letter to the God Ashur' (Frame, RINAP 2, 2021); Paul Zimansky, 'Ecology and Empire: The Structure of the Urartian State' (1985).

nodes.label: The fall of Damascus and Israel
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser III annexed the northern Levant, took Damascus in 732, and turned the coastal and hill kingdoms into provinces. His successors finished the work: after a three-year siege the capital of the Kingdom of Israel, Samaria, fell in 722–720, and Sargon II deported its people east and settled others in their place. The 'ten tribes' of Israel disappear from history here, and Judah is left alone as an Assyrian vassal.
nodes.src: RINAP 1 (Tadmor & Yamada 2011); RINAP 2 (Frame 2021); the Israelite side in 2 Kings 15–17.

nodes.label: Sennacherib and the siege of Jerusalem
nodes.full: In 701 Sennacherib crushed a revolt of the western vassals, stormed the Judahite fortress of Lachish — a siege carved slab by slab across a whole room of his palace — and shut up King Hezekiah in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage'. Then he withdrew without taking the city. The Assyrian annals record heavy tribute and pass over the retreat in silence; the Hebrew Bible attributes the deliverance to a plague sent by the angel of the Lord.
nodes.src: RINAP 3 (Grayson & Novotny 2012); the Lachish reliefs (British Museum); the Judahite account in 2 Kings 18–19 and Isaiah 36–37.

nodes.label: The destruction of Babylon
nodes.full: After years of Babylonian revolt and the loss of a son to Elamite captivity, Sennacherib took Babylon and did what no Mesopotamian king had done to the holy city: he tore it down, dug canals to flood the site, ploughed salt into the ground, and carried the statue of Marduk away. It was regarded across Mesopotamia as monstrous sacrilege, and Assyrian tradition itself later read Sennacherib's murder as the gods' revenge for it.
nodes.src: RINAP 3; the Bavian inscription; the 'Marduk Ordeal' text and the theological reaction analysed by Eckart Frahm.

nodes.label: Egypt and the end of Elam
nodes.full: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal ruled Egypt for two decades, sacking Thebes in 663 and carrying off its wealth — an event the Hebrew prophet Nahum recalls. Ashurbanipal then broke Elam in a series of campaigns, sacked Susa in 646, desecrated its royal tombs, and carried the statue of the goddess Nanaya home after 1,635 years. A famous relief shows him feasting in a garden with the severed head of the Elamite king hanging in a tree.
nodes.src: RINAP 5; the sack of Thebes in Nahum 3:8–10; the Elamite war reliefs from the North Palace (British Museum).

nodes.label: The brothers' war and the fall of Nineveh
nodes.full: The empire's downfall began with a civil war: Ashurbanipal's brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon, rebelled in 652 and was besieged into starvation, dying in the flames in 648. A generation later Nabopolassar's Babylon and Cyaxares' Medes joined forces. Ashur fell in 614; in 612 the allied army stormed Nineveh after a three-month siege and burned it. The last stand at Harran in 610 was the empire's final act.
nodes.src: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' (ABC 3); the war with Shamash-shum-ukin in the Ashurbanipal inscriptions (RINAP 5).

nodes.label: The provincial reform and the eunuch bureaucracy
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser III broke the empire's over-large provinces into small districts, each under a governor he appointed and could recall, and staffed the top of the state with eunuchs — the ša rēši, men who could found no dynasty and had no divided loyalty. A hierarchy of great offices, a royal road with a courier relay, and a paper administration bound the whole to the king. It is the machinery every later Near Eastern empire copied.
nodes.src: Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria' (2015); J. N. Postgate, 'The Land of Assur and the Yoke of Assur' (1992); on eunuchs, Karlheinz Deller.

nodes.label: Mass deportation as demographic engineering
nodes.full: Over three centuries Assyria moved perhaps four and a half million people — not as a punishment but as a policy. Populations were swapped in both directions to sever the tie between a people and its land, resettled with their families, given plots, seed and tools, and made into tax-paying subjects and soldiers. The result was a deliberately blended empire and the spread of Aramaic as its common tongue.
nodes.src: Bustenay Oded, 'Mass Deportations and Deportees in the Neo-Assyrian Empire' (1979).

nodes.label: The loyalty oath of Esarhaddon
nodes.full: In 672 Esarhaddon made every subject and vassal swear an adê — a treaty-oath — to accept his son Ashurbanipal as king and to report any threat to him, backed by pages of graphic curses. Copies were set up in temples across the empire, from Kalhu to a temple in what is now Turkey. The form of the oath — a suzerain, a set of stipulations, blessings and curses — is closely echoed in the biblical book of Deuteronomy.
nodes.src: Simo Parpola & Kazuko Watanabe, 'Neo-Assyrian Treaties and Loyalty Oaths' (SAA 2, 1988); the Tell Tayinat copy in Jacob Lauinger (2012); the Deuteronomy parallel in Hans Ulrich Steymans and Bernard Levinson.

nodes.label: The wall-relief as a propaganda program
nodes.full: From Ashurnasirpal's Northwest Palace onward, the Assyrian kings lined the state rooms of their palaces with carved and painted stone reliefs — kilometres of them — narrating the king's campaigns, hunts and rituals in continuous, aerial-view scenes. The annals were read aloud and buried in the foundations. The empire told and re-told its own story to everyone who walked its halls, in stone meant to last forever.
nodes.src: Irene Winter, 'Royal Rhetoric and the Development of Historical Narrative in Neo-Assyrian Reliefs' (1981); John Malcolm Russell, 'The Writing on the Wall' (1999).

nodes.label: The first professional standing army
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser III turned the seasonal levy into a permanent force — the 'royal cohort', kept in barracks year-round, paid in rations and land, and stiffened with conscripts and deportee auxiliaries. It fielded specialised corps: chariotry, the new cavalry, siege engineers, sappers, a supply train. Armed with iron and drilled to a standard, an Assyrian army of a hundred thousand could march anywhere in the Near East and take any city.
nodes.src: Tamás Dezső, 'The Assyrian Army' I–II (2012); F. M. Fales, 'Guerra e pace in Assiria' (2010).

nodes.label: The intelligence state
nodes.full: A web of royal agents, correspondents and informers reported to the king from every province and every foreign court — troop movements, harvests, prices, plots, rumours. Some three thousand of these letters survive, many with the king's own terse replies. 'The king's word' went out the same channels. Sargon and his successors ran the empire less from a throne than from a desk, reading dispatches.
nodes.src: Simo Parpola, 'The Correspondence of Sargon II' (SAA 1, 1987); Peter Dubovský, 'Hezekiah and the Assyrian Spies' (2006).

nodes.label: The unsolved problem of Babylon
nodes.full: Assyria never found a stable way to rule the older, culturally senior south. Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon took the Babylonian crown personally; Sennacherib tried a son, then a puppet, then destroyed the city; Esarhaddon rebuilt it and split the empire between two of his sons — which produced the civil war that started the collapse. Every arrangement failed, and the failure to solve it was one of the things that killed the empire.
nodes.src: Grant Frame, 'Babylonia 689–627 B.C.: A Political History' (1992); Steven Holloway, 'Aššur is King! Aššur is King!' (2002).

nodes.label: Ashur's war on the world
nodes.full: The empire's official theology held that Ashur's purpose was the extension of 'the land of Ashur' over the whole earth, and that every campaign was a holy war to 'widen the border'. The enemy were 'those who did not know Ashur', aligned with chaos, and their destruction was an act of order and of worship. The king carried the god's standard at the head of the army and rendered him an account on his return.
nodes.src: Beate Pongratz-Leisten, 'Religion and Ideology in Assyria' (2015); Mario Liverani, 'Assyria: The Imperial Mission' (2017).

nodes.label: The king ringed by experts
nodes.full: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal governed inside a cloud of scholars — exorcists, celestial diviners, physicians, haruspices, chief scribes — who wrote to the king daily interpreting omens, prescribing rituals and second-guessing one another. When a truly evil omen threatened the king, a commoner was enthroned as substitute king to absorb it, ruled for up to a hundred days, and was then put to death, the real king having stayed safely 'a farmer' in the meantime.
nodes.src: Simo Parpola, 'Letters from Assyrian and Babylonian Scholars' (SAA 10, 1993); the substitute-king ritual (šar pūhi).

nodes.label: The Assyrian crucible of monotheism
nodes.full: The Assyrian conquest fell hardest on the small kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and it forced a theological reckoning. The eighth-century prophets — Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Micah — read Assyria as the rod of Yahweh, punishing his own people, which meant that the god of a defeated nation could be the god of history itself. Out of that reversal, and the Josianic reform that answered it, grew the ideas that became biblical monotheism.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'Assyria and its Image in the First Isaiah' (JAOS 1983); Mark S. Smith, 'The Early History of God' (2002); Baruch Halpern on the Josianic reform.

nodes.label: The New Year and the humiliation of the king
nodes.full: At the Babylonian New Year festival, the akitu, the king was brought before Marduk, stripped of his crown and sceptre, struck across the face by the high priest, made to kneel and swear that he had not sinned against the city, and only then re-invested. Divine kingship with a built-in ordeal. Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon broke the rite for a generation; its restoration was central to Esarhaddon's rebuilding.
nodes.src: Julye Bidmead, 'The Akitu Festival: Religious Continuity and Royal Legitimation in Mesopotamia' (2002).

nodes.label: Nabu, the god of the written word, rises
nodes.full: Nabu, god of the scribal art and son of Marduk, climbed steadily in importance across the period. His temple at Kalhu, the Ezida, held a library; 'trust in Nabu' became a royal motto stamped on Ashurnasirpal's own statue; his cult spread to every provincial capital. As the empire ran more and more on writing, the god of writing gained accordingly.
nodes.src: Francesco Pomponio, 'Nabû' (Reallexikon der Assyriologie IX); the Ezida temple and its statues from the Nimrud excavations.

nodes.label: A watch kept on the whole sky
nodes.full: The Sargonid state ran a standing network of astrologer-scribes stationed at a dozen cities, each watching the heavens and sending the king reports of every ominous phenomenon with its interpretation from the seventy-tablet canon Enuma Anu Enlil. The same apparatus that gave the king intelligence about his present was used to read the future of the state in the stars — and the reports increasingly note when an event had been correctly predicted.
nodes.src: Hermann Hunger, 'Astrological Reports to Assyrian Kings' (SAA 8, 1992); David Brown, 'Mesopotamian Planetary Astronomy-Astrology' (2000).

nodes.label: The carved narrative wall
nodes.full: The Assyrian palace relief is the largest body of narrative art surviving from the ancient world: carved gypsum slabs, once brightly painted, running for kilometres through the state rooms of the great palaces. Battles, sieges, deportations, hunts and rituals unfold in continuous, high-viewpoint, multi-register scenes, rendered with a documentary precision — every siege engine, every landscape, every foreign costume — and an unflinching depiction of violence in the king's service.
nodes.src: John Malcolm Russell, 'The Writing on the Wall' (1999); Julian Reade, 'Assyrian Sculpture' (1983).

nodes.label: The lion hunt of Ashurbanipal
nodes.full: On the walls of Ashurbanipal's North Palace, lions are released from cages into a closed arena and the king kills them from his chariot and on foot, then pours a libation over the bodies. The carving of the animals — a lioness dragging her paralysed hindquarters, a lion vomiting blood, the taut agony of the dying — is among the most powerful animal art ever made, and the hunt is a ritual: the king mastering the chaos of the wild as he masters the chaos of the nations.
nodes.src: British Museum; Chikako Watanabe, 'Animal Symbolism in Mesopotamia' (2002); Elnathan Weissert on the royal hunt.

nodes.label: The lamassu of the gate
nodes.full: Colossal human-headed, winged bulls and lions — the lamassu, some weighing thirty tons — stood in pairs to either side of the palace and city gates, guardians and imperial statements at once. They were carved with five legs, so that they appear to stand still when seen from the front and to stride forward when seen from the side. Several were smashed with jackhammers and explosives by ISIS at Nineveh, Nimrud and Khorsabad in 2015.
nodes.src: Julian Reade, 'Assyrian Sculpture' (1983); the 2015 destruction documented by UNESCO and the Iraqi authorities.

nodes.label: The Library of Nineveh
nodes.full: Ashurbanipal set out to gather at Nineveh, in one place, the whole of cuneiform writing — omens, epics, hymns, rituals, medicine, lexical lists, letters — sending scribes to Babylonia to copy or simply seize collections. Some thirty thousand tablets and fragments were recovered by Layard and Rassam in the 1850s, among them the eleventh tablet of Gilgamesh with the flood story, whose reading by George Smith in 1872 stunned Victorian London. It is the single greatest source for Mesopotamian civilisation.
nodes.src: Grant Frame & Andrew George, 'The Royal Libraries of Nineveh' (2005); David Damrosch, 'The Buried Book' (2007).

nodes.label: The Nimrud ivories and the imperial style
nodes.full: Thousands of carved ivory plaques — inlays stripped from looted furniture and stored in the palaces and wells of Nimrud — survive in Phoenician, Syrian and Assyrian styles: sphinxes, sacred trees, women at windows, a lioness devouring a boy in a field of gold and lapis, the serene face nicknamed the 'Mona Lisa of Nimrud'. With gold, bronze, glazed brick and the endless 'sacred tree' motif, they are the empire displaying its reach as luxury.
nodes.src: Georgina Herrmann, 'Ivories from Nimrud' (multiple volumes); Max Mallowan, 'Nimrud and its Remains' (1966).

nodes.label: Aramaic and the alphabet
nodes.full: As deportation and conquest made the empire's population overwhelmingly Aramaic-speaking, alphabetic Aramaic written with ink on leather and papyrus became the everyday language of administration alongside cuneiform Akkadian on clay. The reliefs show two scribes side by side at the record of the plunder — one with a stylus and tablet, one with a pen and scroll. It is the beginning of the shift that would, in time, retire cuneiform entirely.
nodes.src: Holger Gzella, 'A Cultural History of Aramaic' (2015); F. M. Fales, 'Aramaic Epigraphs on Clay Tablets of the Neo-Assyrian Period' (1986).

nodes.label: The Library as an attempt at total knowledge
nodes.full: Ashurbanipal's project was intellectually unprecedented: not a working collection but an attempt to hold every kind of written knowledge in one place, organised into numbered series with catch-lines and colophons, catalogued, and checked against 'old' manuscripts. A state that claimed to have mastered the physical world now claimed to have mastered the textual one — and in fixing the canonical editions, it largely decided which of that knowledge would survive.
nodes.src: Eleanor Robson, 'Ancient Knowledge Networks: A Social Geography of Cuneiform Scholarship in First-Millennium Assyria and Babylonia' (2019).

nodes.label: Astronomy becomes predictive
nodes.full: Watching the sky for omens produced, as a by-product, real astronomy. The scribes recognised the cycle on which eclipses recur — the Saros — and could tell the king in advance that a lunar eclipse was coming, and roughly when. From about 747 BC the Babylonian observers began keeping a continuous dated record of the heavens and the weather and prices, the 'Astronomical Diaries', which ran unbroken for seven hundred years.
nodes.src: Hermann Hunger & Abraham Sachs, 'Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia' (1988–); John Steele on early eclipse prediction.

nodes.label: The diagnostic handbook
nodes.full: Under the Sargonids the great medical works were fixed in serialised editions — above all the Diagnostic Handbook, Sakikkû, credited to the editor Esagil-kin-apli and organised as a physical examination from the head downward, matching symptom to divine or natural cause to prognosis. The court physicians' letters — on the king's nosebleeds, his eyes, his depression — show a symptom-based practice working alongside, not instead of, the exorcist's ritual.
nodes.src: Nils Heeßel, 'Babylonisch-assyrische Diagnostik' (2000); JoAnn Scurlock, 'Sourcebook for Ancient Mesopotamian Medicine' (2014).

nodes.label: The world as centre and chaos
nodes.full: The annals and reliefs work out a complete imperial worldview: at the centre, Assyria, ordered and lit by the god; around it, the 'four quarters', a periphery of darkness, rebellion and sub-human enemies whom it is the king's divine duty to conquer and bring into order. The enemy is always the oath-breaker, the chaos-bringer, deserving of what he gets. It is the first fully articulated ideology of empire, and a durable template.
nodes.src: Mario Liverani, 'The Ideology of the Assyrian Empire' (1979) and 'Assyria: The Imperial Mission' (2017).

nodes.label: The Aramaic wisdom undertow — Ahiqar
nodes.full: Even at the empire's height its high culture was Babylonian, its scholars often Babylonian, and its street language Aramaic. The emblem is the story of Ahiqar — the wise counsellor of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon, betrayed by his adopted nephew and vindicated — set at the Assyrian court but composed in Aramaic, in the alphabet, with a string of proverbs at its heart. Assyria fell; Ahiqar was still being copied a thousand years later in a dozen languages.
nodes.src: James Lindenberger, 'The Aramaic Proverbs of Ahiqar' (1983); the earliest copy on a 5th-century papyrus from Elephantine.

nodes.label: The flow to the centre
nodes.full: The empire ran on extraction. Silver, gold, horses, iron, textiles, ivory, cedar, wine and above all people flowed from the conquered periphery to the Assyrian heartland — the annual tribute lists in the annals, the files of gift-bearers on the reliefs. The distinction mattered: madattu, the fixed tribute of a province, versus the one-off 'audience gift' of a still-independent king hoping to stay that way. The Assyrian core grew rich on the yield of the world.
nodes.src: J. N. Postgate, 'Taxation and Conscription in the Assyrian Empire' (1974); F. M. Fales, 'The Neo-Assyrian Period: Economic and Social Structures' (in Frahm, ed., 2017).

nodes.label: The province as a tax unit
nodes.full: Once a kingdom was annexed as a province it paid a standing assessment — grain, livestock, corvée labour and soldiers — into royal storehouses, audited by the governor and the central administration. Tiglath-Pileser III's reform turned Assyrian expansion from a cycle of raiding into a machine of regular, predictable extraction, which is what let the empire pay for its army and its capitals year after year.
nodes.src: Postgate (1974); Karen Radner, 'Money in the Neo-Assyrian Empire' (1999).

nodes.label: Building the capitals
nodes.full: Three times in two centuries an Assyrian king built or rebuilt a capital city — Kalhu, then Dur-Sharrukin from bare ground, then Nineveh on a colossal scale — with the labour of deportees and provincial levies, the timber of Lebanon, the stone of the northern hills, and the metal of the empire. The palaces were economic engines in their own right, employing thousands, and displays: a city raised in a decade was a statement of what the state could command.
nodes.src: David Kertai, 'The Architecture of Late Assyrian Royal Palaces' (2015); the Khorsabad building correspondence (SAA 1, Parpola 1987).

nodes.label: The imperial breadbasket
nodes.full: The empire poured resources into intensifying agriculture in its core and its resettled Jazira: new canals, the introduction of the qanat, dams and reservoirs, olive and vine, and a population swollen with deportees to work the land. Ashurnasirpal and Sennacherib each planted a 'garden' collecting trees, vines and exotic plants from every corner of the empire — part botanical survey, part imperial trophy.
nodes.src: Stephanie Dalley on the Assyrian gardens; Karen Radner on Assyrian agriculture; Simo Parpola on Dur-Sharrukin's countryside.

nodes.label: The Phoenicians and the Arabs under the Assyrian peace
nodes.full: Assyria itself traded little, but it taxed and protected those who did: the Phoenician cities — Tyre, Sidon — that ran the Mediterranean commerce, and the Aramaean and Arab caravans that carried the overland routes. Sargon and his successors pushed those routes into the imperial system: the 'queens of the Arabs' paid tribute in camels and frankincense, and the incense road from South Arabia came, for the first time, within reach of a Mesopotamian power.
nodes.src: María Eugenia Aubet, 'The Phoenicians and the West' (2001); Israel Eph'al, 'The Ancient Arabs' (1982).

nodes.label: The iron economy
nodes.full: The Neo-Assyrian army and economy ran on iron. A single storeroom in Sargon's palace at Khorsabad held some hundred and sixty tons of iron in ingots and unfinished tools — a state reserve. Iron tools transformed clearing, ploughing and quarrying; iron weapons armed a hundred thousand men; and control of the ore of the Zagros and Anatolia was a strategic concern that shaped Assyrian campaigns.
nodes.src: The Khorsabad iron hoard from Gordon Loud's excavations (OIP 40, 1936); Jane Waldbaum, 'From Bronze to Iron' (1978).

nodes.label: Siege warfare as engineering
nodes.full: The Assyrian siege was a coordinated engineering operation, carved in detail on the reliefs: an earthen ramp built up to the wall, a wheeled battering ram inside an armoured shed with a water-tank against fire, siege towers, sappers undermining the foundations, archers giving covering fire, and the escalade. No city in the Near East could count on holding out. The Lachish relief is a whole room devoted to one such assault.
nodes.src: Israel Eph'al, 'The City Besieged: Siege and its Manifestations in the Ancient Near East' (2009); the Lachish reliefs (British Museum).

nodes.label: Sennacherib's water system
nodes.full: To water Nineveh and its gardens Sennacherib built a network of more than fifty kilometres of canals from the Zagros foothills, including at Jerwan a stone aqueduct nearly three hundred metres long carrying the channel across a valley on arches, lined with waterproof cement — the oldest aqueduct known. He also claims to have raised water by a bronze screw or 'great cylinder' cast by a new method: the passage is disputed but may describe the device later called the Archimedes screw.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen & Seton Lloyd, 'Sennacherib's Aqueduct at Jerwan' (OIP 24, 1935); the water-screw argument in Stephanie Dalley, 'The Mystery of the Hanging Garden of Babylon' (2013).

nodes.label: The mounted archer
nodes.full: The Neo-Assyrians developed true cavalry. Early reliefs show a mounted archer paired with a second rider who holds both horses' reins so the first can shoot; within a century the archer controls his own horse with his knees and rides alone. It was a new arm — faster and more flexible than the chariot on broken ground — and the empires that followed, Persia above all and then the steppe, took it much further.
nodes.src: Robert Drews, 'Early Riders: The Beginnings of Mounted Warfare in Asia and Europe' (2004); Tamás Dezső, 'The Assyrian Army' (2012).

nodes.label: Moving and carving the colossus
nodes.full: Sennacherib's reliefs show the whole operation: a thirty-ton block of stone quarried, roughed into a lamassu, dragged on a sledge over log rollers by hundreds of hauliers with the king watching, levered up an earthen ramp, and set in the gateway. Rock reliefs at Bavian and Maltai advertise the same message on cliff faces in the mountains. Monumental logistics, performed in public, were a demonstration of what the state could compel.
nodes.src: John Malcolm Russell, 'Sennacherib's Palace Without Rival' (1991); the transport reliefs from the South-West Palace.

nodes.label: The relief program as an industry
nodes.full: Lining a palace with reliefs was mass production: gypsum quarried and floated downriver, slabs cut and set against the mud-brick walls, a master's design laid out, teams of carvers working sections to a template, painters adding colour, and scribes cutting the cuneiform captions. Acres of finished wall were produced for each new palace in a few years — an art program run with the organisation of a public works.
nodes.src: John Malcolm Russell, 'The Writing on the Wall' (1999); Pauline Albenda on relief production.

nodes.label: The great kings of the Iron Age
nodes.full: Assyria dominated a world of other powers rather than sharing one: Urartu in the northern mountains, Egypt under its Kushite and then Saite kings, Elam in the east, Phrygia under a king the Assyrians called Mita — Midas — and, beyond them, the fringes Assyria was just beginning to touch: Cyprus, the raiding 'Ionian' Greeks of the Cilician coast, the Medes, and the Arabs of the desert. It was a system with a hegemon, not a balance.
nodes.src: Trevor Bryce, 'The World of the Neo-Hittite Kingdoms' (2012); the 'Ionians' and Cyprus in the Sargon inscriptions (Frame, RINAP 2, 2021).

nodes.label: The deportations that mixed the Near East
nodes.full: Three centuries of two-way mass deportation permanently reshaped the ethnic map. Israelites went east and vanished into Mesopotamia and Media; Babylonians, Elamites, Arabs and Anatolians were planted in the Levant and the Assyrian core; and Aramaic, the deportees' common tongue, spread until it was the everyday language from the Zagros to Egypt. The 'melting pot' of the later Near East is in large part an Assyrian creation.
nodes.src: Bustenay Oded, 'Mass Deportations and Deportees in the Neo-Assyrian Empire' (1979); the linguistic outcome in Holger Gzella (2015).

nodes.label: The Phoenicians pushed west
nodes.full: As Assyria squeezed the Levantine coast harder for tribute, the Phoenician cities looked west for room and revenue. The traditional foundation of Carthage falls in 814, and through the eighth century Phoenician colonies and trading posts spread along the North African coast, through Sicily and Sardinia, and to Cadiz beyond the Straits. The Assyrian pressure on Tyre and Sidon helped launch the movement that would seed the western Mediterranean.
nodes.src: María Eugenia Aubet, 'The Phoenicians and the West' (2001); the 'Assyrian push' hypothesis and its critics.

nodes.label: Assyria and the Arabs
nodes.full: The Neo-Assyrian records give the first sustained account of the Arabian tribes: the 'queens of the Arabs' — Zabibe, Samsi, Te'elhunu — paying tribute in camels, gold and frankincense; the oasis of Adummatu (Dumat al-Jandal) taken and its gods carried off; and campaigns by Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal deep into the desert against the tribes and their sanctuaries. The incense road and the camel nomads entered the historical record here.
nodes.src: Israel Eph'al, 'The Ancient Arabs: Nomads on the Borders of the Fertile Crescent, 9th–5th Centuries B.C.' (1982); see the folio qedar-853bc-330bc.

nodes.label: The Median alliance and the fall
nodes.full: The Medes were an Iranian people the Assyrians had raided for horses for two centuries. In the 620s they coalesced into a kingdom under Cyaxares, and — allied with Nabopolassar's newly independent Babylon — turned on their old tormentor. The joint campaigns of 614–609 destroyed Assyria utterly. It was the first time an Iranian power decided the fate of Mesopotamia; within a century the Persians would rule it all.
nodes.src: The 'Fall of Nineveh Chronicle' (ABC 3); Herodotus I.102–106; Robert Rollinger on the historical Medes.

nodes.label: The empire's long afterlife
nodes.full: Assyria was remembered two ways. As a warning — the archetype of tyranny and hubris in Nahum, Jonah and Isaiah, and the fantastical 'Ninus and Semiramis' of the Greeks. And as a model — the Persians and every later Near Eastern empire copied its provinces, roads, deportations and royal ideology. The cities themselves were lost so completely that Xenophon marched past Nineveh in 401 without knowing whose ruins they were, until Botta and Layard dug them up in the 1840s.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'The Fall of Assyria in Comparative Ancient Perspective' (1997); Xenophon, 'Anabasis' III.4; Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Conquest of Assyria' (1996) on the rediscovery.

nodes.label: The first empire of the whole Fertile Crescent
nodes.full: At its height under Ashurbanipal, Assyria ruled from the first cataract of the Nile to the Zagros mountains, from Cyprus to the head of the Persian Gulf — well over a million square kilometres and perhaps twenty million people. It was the largest state the world had yet produced, and the first time a single power held the entire Fertile Crescent at once. The word 'empire', in its later sense, is modelled on this.
nodes.src: Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria' (2015); the extent mapped in Eckart Frahm (ed.), 'A Companion to Assyria' (2017).

nodes.label: The transformed heartland
nodes.full: The tribute and labour of the world were poured into the Assyrian core. The triangle of Assur, Nineveh, Kalhu, Arbela and the new Dur-Sharrukin became a landscape of successive capitals, palaces of acres, canal networks, terraced gardens stocked with plants from every province, and farmland worked by resettled deportees. No region of the ancient world was as densely built and as heavily urbanised.
nodes.src: David Kertai, 'The Architecture of Late Assyrian Royal Palaces' (2015); the heartland survey work of Tony Wilkinson and Jason Ur.

nodes.label: Drought, over-reach and the speed of the fall
nodes.full: Why the greatest power in the world vanished in twenty years is still argued. Tree-ring and cave records point to a severe mid-seventh-century drought striking the rain-fed heartland; the empire was over-extended and structurally fragile, needing perpetual conquest to fund itself; the civil war and the succession disputes gutted it from within; and Babylon and the Medes struck at exactly the wrong moment. What is not in doubt is the totality — from superpower to non-existence.
nodes.src: Adam Schneider & Selim Adalı, 'No harvest was reaped: demographic and climatic factors in the decline of the Neo-Assyrian Empire' (2014); Eckart Frahm on the collapse.

nodes.label: The empty land
nodes.full: After 609 the Assyrian heartland was so thoroughly emptied and its cities so completely abandoned that Assyria as a state was simply gone. When Xenophon's Ten Thousand marched past the ruins of Nimrud and Nineveh in 401, they recorded them as the deserted walls of a vanished people whose name they did not know. 'Assyrian' survived as a rural identity and, much later, a Christian one — but the empire left no successor and, for two thousand years, almost no memory on the ground.
nodes.src: Xenophon, 'Anabasis' III.4.7–12; Peter Machinist, 'The Fall of Assyria in Comparative Ancient Perspective' (1997).

nodes.label: The deportee's road
nodes.full: The reliefs show them: families on the march with ox-carts and bundles, women and children walking, an Assyrian soldier alongside. At the far end lay resettlement — a plot of land, seed, tools, and a tax obligation — in a province chosen so that they would be strangers among strangers, unable to combine. Within a generation their children were Assyrian subjects and, often, Assyrian soldiers. The policy destroyed communities and built an empire out of the pieces.
nodes.src: Bustenay Oded, 'Mass Deportations and Deportees' (1979); the deportation scenes on the Sennacherib and Tiglath-Pileser reliefs.

nodes.label: The eunuch at the heart of the state
nodes.full: A boy castrated for a career gave up the possibility of a dynasty and gained, in exchange, the total trust of the king. Eunuchs — the ša rēši — served as generals, provincial governors, treasurers and the king's closest advisers, and they are easy to spot on the reliefs: beardless, standing immediately behind the throne. They were the un-hereditary, un-divided-loyalty backbone of the imperial administration.
nodes.src: Karlheinz Deller on Neo-Assyrian eunuchs; Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria' (2015).

nodes.label: The scholar of the court letters
nodes.full: The exorcists and star-scribes who advised Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal wrote to the king constantly — reporting an eclipse and what it meant, prescribing a ritual to avert a bad omen, warning that a rival colleague's reading was wrong, complaining that they had not been paid or promoted. Their letters, some twelve hundred of them, open a window on an anxious, competitive, intimate world at the top of the empire.
nodes.src: Simo Parpola, 'Letters from Assyrian and Babylonian Scholars' (SAA 10, 1993).

nodes.label: The soldier of the standing army
nodes.full: A professional in the royal cohort, or a deportee auxiliary armed and drilled to the same standard: an iron-scaled coat, a pointed helmet, a heavy spear and a tall shield, or a bow. He served year-round, was paid in rations and a plot of land, and took a share of the plunder and the captives when a campaign went well. The reliefs show him in endless disciplined files — the human substance of a state organised for war.
nodes.src: Tamás Dezső, 'The Assyrian Army' (2012); F. M. Fales, 'Guerra e pace in Assiria' (2010).

nodes.label: The provincial subject
nodes.full: A farmer or townsman in an annexed kingdom paid the grain-tax and turned out for the labour-levy, watched deportees arrive from somewhere else and his own neighbours march away, heard the king's latest annals read out at the governor's residence, and slowly shifted from his own language to Aramaic. If the empire's grip loosened — a lost battle, a disputed succession — he was a candidate for the next revolt, and for the reprisal that followed it.
nodes.src: F. M. Fales, 'The Neo-Assyrian Period: Economic and Social Structures' (in Frahm, ed., 2017).
